analysis.one_liner: Gives tax credits for donations that pay private school tuition for low-income students.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one senator with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on its first day, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal tax credit, dollar for dollar, for donations to nonprofit "scholarship granting organizations" that pay private school tuition for children from households earning up to 250% of the federal poverty line. Individual donors could claim up to $4,500 a year and corporations up to $100,000. The organizations would have to give out at least 90% of what they receive, verify family income, and submit to audits, and private schools taking the money would have to report student test results. The bill was introduced on the Senate's first day of the 116th Congress, sent to the Finance Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income families whose children could receive scholarships covering private elementary and secondary school tuition, and the donors — individuals and corporations — who would get a federal tax credit repaying every dollar they give.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income families seeking private school seats

how_it_helps.text: Children from households earning up to 250% of the federal poverty guidelines could get scholarships covering tuition and other qualified elementary and secondary school expenses at schools that charge tuition.
Donors would get a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit — up to $4,500 for individuals and $100,000 for corporations — so contributing to a scholarship fund would cost them nothing out of pocket.

The bill includes guardrails: scholarship organizations must distribute at least 90% of receipts, verify family income, obtain independent audits, and accept an excise tax penalty if they fail to distribute; receiving schools must follow state anti-discrimination, health, safety, and background-check laws and report scholarship students' standardized test results, with annual federal evaluations of academic outcomes made public.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through revenue given up for the credits; because the credit is dollar-for-dollar, the Treasury would effectively cover the full cost of most donations, and that money would otherwise go to the general fund.

drawbacks.text: A dollar-for-dollar credit makes donations free to the donor, so the federal government would finance most of the roughly $4,500-per-person and $100,000-per-corporation contributions, transferring money from the general Treasury to private school tuition with no offsetting revenue.

The benefit reaches only families who can actually obtain a seat at a tuition-charging private school in their area; it does nothing for students in places without them, and it diverts federal dollars toward private schools rather than the public school system that serves all children.

Donations could be earmarked neither to a particular student nor a specific school, and organizations must serve students at more than one school, but the credit still creates a new federally subsidized channel that private schools and scholarship intermediaries would depend on and promote.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real, targeted benefit: low-income children would get money for private school tuition, with unusually detailed auditing, income verification, and testing requirements attached. But the mechanism is expensive — a dollar-for-dollar federal credit means taxpayers, not donors, bear the cost of the contributions — and the help is limited to families near a willing private school. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how one values private school alternatives against the federal revenue that could instead support public schools. The design is more accountable than many school-choice tax credit proposals, but the cost structure still favors donors and tuition-charging schools.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on the first day of the Congress, and the committee never took it up, so it expired without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the Educational Opportunities Act on January 3, 2019, the opening day of the 116th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
No senator joined as a cosponsor — the cosponsor list shows zero for the entire two years.
The bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, never having received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: no federal revenue was committed to private school tuition credits, public school funding was untouched, and the donors and private schools that would have benefited from the credit gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the Senate's first day of the 116th Congress and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 3, 2019 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote; its only support was a single Republican sponsor, and no Democrat or other member signed on as a cosponsor during the two years it sat in committee.

industries.note: Tuition-charging private schools would receive federally subsidized tuition from scholarship students, a new revenue stream — provided they follow state anti-discrimination and safety laws and report test results. Families without access to a nearby private school would see no benefit.

The bill creates a new class of tax-exempt intermediaries that would permanently sit between federal tax credits and school tuition, with mandatory audits and a 90% distribution requirement but a built-in role as the channel for the subsidy.

Donors would get a dollar-for-dollar federal credit — up to $100,000 for corporations — meaning a contribution costs them nothing while the Treasury covers it; the money could alternatively fund public services directly.

Public schools would not lose dollars directly, but the bill spends federal revenue on private tuition rather than on the system that educates the vast majority of children, and subsidizes movement of some students out of public schools.
